Luke — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Luke is generally believed to have been a physician and a companion of the apostle Paul.

Henry considers Luke's style and familiarity with Jewish rites and customs evidence that he was Jewish. At the same time, he considers Luke's Greek name and knowledge of the Greek language evidence of a Gentile background.

These apparently conflicting observations are retained as the commentator's own statements, rather than harmonized by an undocumented editorial decision.

Luke first appears in Acts 16:10–11, where he joined Paul at Troas. Henry says that he accompanied Paul to Jerusalem and was also with him during his travels and imprisonment in Rome.

The Gospel appears intended to replace the numerous deficient and unreliable accounts then circulating.

Its purpose is to provide an authentic and inspired account of Jesus' life, miracles and teaching, based on the testimony of people who heard and saw those events themselves.

Luke's preface (verses 1–4)

Luke did not intend to write about questions on which Christians may safely disagree or remain uncertain.

He wrote about the things that are, and ought to be, firmly believed.

The teaching of Christ is what the wisest and best people have confidently entrusted their souls to, with deep satisfaction.

The great events on which our hope depends were recorded from the testimony of those who were eyewitnesses from the beginning and ministers of the word.

Their understanding was brought to completeness through divine inspiration.

Zechariah and Elizabeth (verses 5–25)

The parents of John the Baptist were sinners, like everyone else, and were justified and saved in the same way as other believers.

Yet they were distinguished by their genuine godliness and integrity.

They had no children, and Elizabeth's advanced age meant they could no longer expect a child by ordinary means.

While Zechariah burned incense in the temple, the people were gathered outside in prayer.

All prayer offered to God can be accepted and answered only through Christ's intercession in the heavenly temple.

We must pray ourselves, earnestly and from the heart, if we hope to share in that intercession.

Even our best prayers receive an answer of peace only through the mediation of Christ, who always lives to intercede.

Zechariah had often prayed for a child.

Those prayers were not forgotten: prayers offered in faith are kept before God, and he may answer requests made in youth when we have reached old age.

Gifts received through prayer bring a special kind of happiness.

The promised son would be a means of turning many people to God and preparing them to receive Christ's gospel.

He would go before the Savior with courage, zeal, holiness and detachment from earthly pleasures and ambitions.

The disobedient would be turned toward the wisdom of righteous ancestors—or, more fully, toward the wisdom of the Righteous One who was coming.

Zechariah heard the angel's promise but spoke in unbelief.

God rightly made him unable to speak because he had objected to the divine word.

Yet even that correction was kind: it prevented further expressions of unbelief and strengthened his faith.

When discipline helps us trust God's word more fully, we have no reason to complain.

Even sincere believers may dishonor the Lord through unbelief. Their mouths are sometimes closed in confusion when they should be open in grateful praise.

We should recognize the Lord's merciful attention when he looks upon us with compassion and acts for our good.

Gabriel announces Jesus' birth to Mary (verses 26–38)

Here we learn about the mother of our Lord.

We should not pray to Mary, but we should praise God for the favor he showed her.

Christ's birth was necessarily miraculous.

The angel greeted Mary as someone specially chosen and favored by the Most High, receiving an honor that generations of Jewish mothers had long hoped for.

The greeting troubled her, but the angel assured her that God had shown her favor.

She would bear a son named Jesus, the Son of the Most High, sharing in divine nature and perfection.

How precious the name Jesus—Savior—is to sinners who know their need!

We often fail to run to him because we do not recognize either our own poverty and peril or his immeasurable riches.

A person truly convinced of sin's guilt and the judgment it deserves would continually ask: Is the Savior mine?

Such a person would willingly overcome anything that hindered coming to him.

Mary's response expressed humble wonder and faith, not a demand for a sign.

Great indeed is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh (1 Timothy 3:16, the cited source wording).

Christ's human nature was brought into being in a way appropriate for its union with the divine nature.

Like Mary, we should bring our desires into agreement with God's word.

In every difficulty, remember that nothing is impossible with God.

When we hear his promises, we should turn them into prayers:

I am the Lord's willing servant; let it happen to me according to your word.

Mary visits Elizabeth (verses 39–56)

People in whom God has begun the work of grace benefit from sharing their experience with one another.

When Mary arrived, Elizabeth recognized the presence of the one who would become mother of the great Redeemer.

Filled with the Holy Spirit, she declared Mary and the child she carried greatly blessed because God had honored and loved them.

Mary, strengthened by Elizabeth's words and herself moved by the Holy Spirit, responded with joy, wonder and gratitude.

Mary knew she was a sinner who needed a Savior.

She could rejoice in God only through the salvation provided in the promised Messiah.

Those who recognize their need of Christ and hunger for righteousness and life in him receive the best gifts.

He fills them with spiritual blessings until they are satisfied.

The poor in spirit will find their longing fulfilled, while those who imagine they need nothing will depart empty.

John the Baptist is born (verses 57–66)

John's birth brought joy throughout the family.

His name, Johanan, was associated by Henry with “gracious”, because John would introduce the gospel of Christ, in which God's grace shines so clearly.

Zechariah's speech returned.

Unbelief had closed his mouth; believing opened it again.

He believed, and therefore he spoke.

When God opens our lips, we ought to praise him.

It would be better to lack speech than to possess it and never use it to glorify God.

The Lord's hand was with John.

God can work in the lives of infants in ways we cannot fully explain.

We should notice what he does and wait to see what follows.

Zechariah's prophetic song (verses 67–80)

Zechariah prophesied about the Messiah's kingdom and salvation.

The gospel brings light.

In John's ministry, the dawn began to break, growing brighter until the fullness of daylight.

The gospel reveals what was hidden: the knowledge of God's glory in the face of Jesus Christ.

It revives those sitting in death's shadow, like condemned prisoners in a dark dungeon.

It guides our feet onto the way of peace, the path that will at last bring us to peace (Romans 3:17).

John showed strong faith, vigorous and holy affections, and freedom from excessive fear or love of the world.

Through those years he grew ready for useful work, though he lived privately until he appeared publicly as the Messiah's forerunner.

Let us pursue peace with everyone, while also seeking peace with God and with our consciences.

If God calls us to remain unknown to the world, we can still grow diligently in the grace of Jesus Christ.

Luke
This evangelist is generally supposed to have been a physician, and a companion of the apostle Paul. The style of his writings, and his acquaintance with the Jewish rites and usages, sufficiently show that he was a Jew, while his knowledge of the Greek language and his name, speak his Gentile origin. He is first mentioned [Acts.16.10] Ac 16:10, [Acts.16.11] 11, as with Paul at Troas, whence he attended him to Jerusalem, and was with him in his voyage, and in his imprisonment at Rome. This Gospel appears to be designed to supersede many defective and unauthentic narratives in circulation, and to give a genuine and inspired account of the life, miracles, and doctrines of our Lord, learned from those who heard and witnessed his discourses and miracles.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The Preface. | (1-4) |
Zacharias and Elisabeth. | (5-25) |
Christ's birth announced. | (26-38) |
Interview of Mary and Elisabeth. | (39-56) |

The song of Zacharias. | (67-80) |
Verses 1-4
Luke will not write of things about which Christians may safely differ from one another, and hesitate within themselves; but the things which are, and ought to be surely believed. The doctrine of Christ is what the wisest and best of men have ventured their souls upon with confidence and satisfaction. And the great events whereon our hopes depend, have been recorded by those who were from the beginning eye-witnesses and ministers of the word, and who were perfected in their understanding of them through Divine inspiration.
[Luke.1.5-Luke.1.25]
Verses 5-25
The father and mother of John the Baptist were sinners as all are, and were justified and saved in the same way as others; but they were eminent for piety and integrity. They had no children, and it could not be expected that Elisabeth should have any in her old age. While Zacharias was burning incense in the temple, the whole multitude of the people were praying without. All the prayers we offer up to God, are acceptable and successful only by Christ's intercession in the temple of God above. We cannot expect an interest therein if we do not pray, and pray with our spirits, and are not earnest in prayer. Nor can we expect that the best of our prayers should gain acceptance, and bring an answer of peace, but through the mediation of Christ, who ever lives, making intercession. The prayers Zacharias often made, received an answer of peace. Prayers of faith are filed in heaven, and are not forgotten. Prayers made when we were young and entering into the world, may be answered when we are old and going out of the world. Mercies are doubly sweet that are given in answer to prayer. Zacharias shall have a son in his old age, who shall be instrumental in the conversion of many souls to God, and preparing them to receive the gospel of Christ. He shall go before Him with courage, zeal, holiness, and a mind dead to earthly interests and pleasures. The disobedient and rebellious would be brought back to the wisdom of their righteous forefathers, or rather, brought to attend to the wisdom of that Just One who was coming among them. Zacharias heard all that the angel said; but his unbelief spake. In striking him dumb, God dealt justly with him, because he had objected against God's word. We may admire the patience of God towards us. God dealt kindly with him, for thus he prevented his speaking any more distrustful, unbelieving words. Thus also God confirmed his faith. If by the rebukes we are under for our sin, we are brought to give the more credit to the word of God, we have no reason to complain. Even real believers are apt to dishonour God by unbelief; and their mouths are stopped in silence and confusion, when otherwise they would have been praising God with joy and gratitude. In God's gracious dealings with us we ought to observe his gracious regards to us. He has looked on us with compassion and favour, and therefore has thus dealt with us.
[Luke.1.26-Luke.1.38]
Verses 26-38
We have here an account of the mother of our Lord; though we are not to pray to her, yet we ought to praise God for her. Christ must be born miraculously. The angel's address means only, Hail, thou that art the especially chosen and favoured of the Most High, to attain the honour Jewish mothers have so long desired. This wondrous salutation and appearance troubled Mary. The angel then assured her that she had found favour with God, and would become the mother of a son whose name she should call Jesus, the Son of the Highest, one in a nature and perfection with the Lord God. JESUS! the name that refreshes the fainting spirits of humbled sinners; sweet to speak and sweet to hear, Jesus, a Saviour! We know not his riches and our own poverty, therefore we run not to him; we perceive not that we are lost and perishing, therefore a Saviour is a word of little relish. Were we convinced of the huge mass of guilt that lies upon us, and the wrath that hangs over us for it, ready to fall upon us, it would be our continual thought, Is the Saviour mine? And that we might find him so, we should trample on all that hinders our way to him. Mary's reply to the angel was the language of faith and humble admiration, and she asked no sign for the confirming her faith. Without controversy, great was the mystery of godliness, God manifest in the flesh, [1Tim.3.16] 1Ti 3:16. Christ's human nature must be produced so, as it was fit that should be which was to be taken into union with the Divine nature. And we must, as Mary here, guide our desires by the word of God. In all conflicts, let us remember that with God nothing is impossible; and as we read and hear his promises, let us turn them into prayers, Behold the willing servant of the Lord; let it be unto me according to thy word.
[Luke.1.39-Luke.1.56]
Verses 39-56
It is very good for those who have the work of grace begun in their souls, to communicate one to another. On Mary's arrival, Elisabeth was conscious of the approach of her who was to be the mother of the great Redeemer. At the same time she was filled with the Holy Ghost, and under his influence declared that Mary and her expected child were most blessed and happy, as peculiarly honoured of and dear to the Most High God. Mary, animated by Elisabeth's address, and being also under the influence of the Holy Ghost, broke out into joy, admiration, and gratitude. She knew herself to be a sinner who needed a Saviour, and that she could no otherwise rejoice in God than as interested in his salvation through the promised Messiah. Those who see their need of Christ, and are desirous of righteousness and life in him, he fills with good things, with the best things; and they are abundantly satisfied with the blessings he gives. He will satisfy the desires of the poor in spirit who long for spiritual blessings, while the self-sufficient shall be sent empty away.
[Luke.1.57-Luke.1.66]
Verses 57-66
In these verses we have an account of the birth of John the Baptist, and the great joy among all the relations of the family. He shall be called Johanan, or "Gracious," because he shall bring in the gospel of Christ, wherein God's grace shines most bright. Zacharias recovered his speech. Unbelief closed his mouth, and believing opened it again: he believers, therefore he speaks. When God opens our lips, our mouths must show forth his praise; and better be without speech, than not use it in praising God. It is said, The hand of the Lord was working with John. God has ways of working on children in their infancy, which we cannot account for. We should observe the dealings of God, and wait the event.
[Luke.1.67-Luke.1.80]
Verses 67-80
Zacharias uttered a prophecy concerning the kingdom and salvation of the Messiah. The gospel brings light with it; in it the day dawns. In John the Baptist it began to break, and increased apace to the perfect day. The gospel is discovering; it shows that about which we were utterly in the dark; it is to give light to those that sit in darkness, the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. It is reviving; it brings light to those that sit in the shadow of death, as condemned prisoners in the dungeon. It is directing; it is to guide our feet in the way of peace, into that way which will bring us to peace at last, [Rom.3.17] Ro 3:17. John gave proofs of strong faith, vigorous and holy affections, and of being above the fear and love of the world. Thus he ripened for usefulness; but he lived a retired life, till he came forward openly as the forerunner of the Messiah. Let us follow peace with all men, as well as seek peace with God and our own consciences. And if it be the will of God that we live unknown to the world, still let us diligently seek to grow strong in the grace of Jesus Christ.

Christ is born (verses 1–7)

The fullness of time had come.

God sent his Son, born of a woman and born under the law.

The circumstances of Jesus' birth were extraordinarily humble.

He was born where travelers lodged, as a temporary guest in the world. His brief earthly stay teaches us to regard ourselves as sojourners here too.

Through sin, humanity had become like an abandoned newborn—helpless and without hope. Christ entered a condition resembling ours.

He knew how reluctant people are to live in humble homes, wear ordinary clothing or eat simple meals.

He knew how parents desire to decorate and indulge their children, how readily poor people envy the rich, and how often rich people look down upon the poor.

Yet when we look in faith at the Son of God made human and lying in a manger, our vanity, ambition and envy are challenged.

We can hardly contemplate that scene properly and still make earthly greatness the object of our desires for ourselves or our children.

Angels announce the birth to shepherds (verses 8–20)

Angels announced the Savior's birth, but they were sent to humble, devout and hardworking shepherds.

These shepherds were carrying out their ordinary occupation, watching their sheep.

Faithful work does not put us beyond the reach of God's gracious visits. We may remain close to him while carrying out an honest calling.

The glory of this work belongs to God: Glory to God in the highest.

All God's works display his glory, but the redemption of the world displays his glory in the highest way.

God's goodwill toward humanity, made known through the coming of the Messiah, brought peace into this world.

Here peace means all the good that flows to us because Christ took our nature upon himself.

An innumerable company of angels confirmed this welcome message.

The shepherds hurried to the place.

Having found what they were told to expect, they spread the good news about the child who was the Savior, Christ the Lord.

Mary carefully kept and considered everything that happened.

These events strengthened her devotion.

We, too, would avoid many errors in judgment and behavior if we pondered more deeply what God has revealed about his Son.

The announcement remains good news for us: a Savior, Christ the Lord, has been born.

Jesus is circumcised and presented in the temple (verses 21–24)

Our Lord Jesus was not born in sin.

Unlike sinners, he did not need the death of a corrupt nature or renewal toward holiness that circumcision symbolized.

For him, the ordinance anticipated his coming perfect obedience to the whole law, through suffering and temptation, even to death on our behalf.

After forty days, Mary went to the temple to offer the sacrifices appointed for purification.

Joseph also presented the holy child Jesus.

As a firstborn son, he was to be dedicated to the Lord and redeemed according to the law.

Let us similarly present our children to the Lord who gave them to us, asking him to rescue them from sin and death and make them holy to himself.

Simeon prophesies about Jesus (verses 25–35)

The same Spirit who sustained Simeon's hope now brought that hope to joyful fulfillment.

Those who desire to see Christ should seek him where he makes himself known.

Simeon confessed that the child he held was the Savior himself—the salvation God had appointed.

He was ready to leave the world.

How small this world appears to someone who holds Christ and beholds salvation!

Simeon's words show the comfort of a godly person's death.

Such a person departs at peace with God, at peace in conscience, and at peace with the thought of death.

Those who have welcomed Christ can welcome death.

Joseph and Mary marveled at what was said about Jesus.

Simeon's prophecy also gave them reason to rejoice with reverent trembling.

Jesus, his truth and his people continue to be spoken against.

His teaching becomes a test that reveals human character.

Some people's hidden good desires are exposed when they embrace him.

Other people's hidden corruption is revealed through their opposition to him.

Human beings will be judged according to their heart's response to Christ.

Jesus would be a suffering Savior, and his mother would suffer too because of her close relationship and love for him.

Anna speaks about Jesus (verses 36–40)

There was much wrong in the religious community of that period, but God had not left himself without witnesses.

Anna lived at the temple or attended it constantly.

She was devoted to prayer and served God in everything.

People to whom Jesus has been revealed have good reason to thank the Lord and tell others about him, as she did.

The examples of Simeon and Anna should encourage older believers.

Their gray hair is a crown of honor when they continue in the way of righteousness.

Before our lips are silenced by death, let us use them to praise our Redeemer.

It was fitting for Christ to be made like his brothers and sisters in every respect.

He passed through infancy and childhood as other children do, yet without sin and with clear signs of his divine nature.

By the Spirit of God all his powers functioned perfectly.

Other children have foolishness bound up in their hearts, as their actions and words reveal. Jesus, by contrast, was full of wisdom.

Everything he said and did was appropriate and wise, far beyond his years.

While other children reveal the corruption of fallen nature, he displayed only the grace of God.

Jesus speaks with teachers in the temple (verses 41–52)

Children honor Christ when they attend public worship.

Jesus' earthly parents remained for all seven days of the festival.

It is good to stay to the end of worship rather than hurry away from holy duties.

Those who have lost the comfort of fellowship with Christ and the assurance of belonging to him should ask where, when and how they lost these blessings and retrace their steps.

They should seek him where he has promised to make himself known.

Mary and Joseph found Jesus in the temple, where teachers of the law instructed their students.

He listened, asked questions and answered questions with remarkable wisdom.

Young people should seek the truth of God, attend the teaching of the gospel and ask their elders and teachers thoughtful questions that will deepen their understanding.

Those who seek Jesus sorrowfully can find him again with greater joy.

Jesus explained that he must be in his Father's house, attending to his Father's business.

All God's children should likewise make the Father's work their first concern, letting other matters yield to it when necessary.

Yet although Jesus was the Son of God, he submitted to his earthly parents.

How can ordinary people justify disobedience to their parents when the divine Son obeyed his?

We may fail to understand human speech because it is unclear. But we must not dismiss God's words as though they were unreliable.

What first seems difficult may later become plain.

Even the greatest and wisest can learn from this extraordinary Child that true greatness includes knowing our proper position, fulfilling our calling and refusing pleasures that conflict with our duties.

At the end of forty days, Mary went up to the temple to offer the appointed sacrifices for her purification. How poor does this world look to one that has Christ in his arms, and salvation in his view! See here, how comfortable is the death of a good man; he departs in peace with God, peace with his own conscience, in peace with death. Those that have welcomed Christ, may welcome death. Joseph and Mary marvelled at the things which were spoken of this Child. Simeon shows them likewise, what reason they had to rejoice with trembling. And Jesus, his doctrine, and people, are still spoken against; his truth and holiness are still denied and blasphemed; his preached word is still the touchstone of men's characters. The secret good affections in the minds of some, will be revealed by their embracing Christ; the secret corruptions of others will be revealed by their enmity to Christ. Men will be judged by the thoughts of their hearts concerning Christ. He shall be a suffering Jesus; his mother shall suffer with him, because of the nearness of her relation and affection.
[Luke.2.36-Luke.2.40]
Verses 36-40
There was much evil then in the church, yet God left not himself without witness. Anna always dwelt in, or at least attended at, the temple. She was always in a praying spirit; gave herself to prayer, and in all things she served God. Those to whom Christ is made known, have great reason to thank the Lord. She taught others concerning him. Let the example of the venerable saints, Simeon and Anna, give courage to those whose hoary heads are, like theirs, a crown of glory, being found in the way of righteousness. The lips soon to be silent in the grave, should be showing forth the praises of the Redeemer. In all things it became Christ to be made like unto his brethren, therefore he passed through infancy and childhood as other children, yet without sin, and with manifest proofs of the Divine nature in him. By the Spirit of God all his faculties performed their offices in a manner not seen in any one else. Other children have foolishness bound in their hearts, which appears in what they say or do, but he was filled with wisdom, by the influence of the Holy Ghost; every thing he said and did, was wisely said and wisely done, above his years. Other children show the corruption of their nature; nothing but the grace of God was upon him.
[Luke.2.41-Luke.2.52]
Verses 41-52
It is for the honour of Christ that children should attend on public worship. His parents did not return till they had stayed all the seven days of the feast. It is well to stay to the end of an ordinance, as becomes those who say, It is good to be here. Those that have lost their comforts in Christ, and the evidences of their having a part in him, must bethink themselves where, and when, and how they lost them, and must turn back again. Those that would recover their lost acquaintance with Christ, must go to the place in which he has put his name; there they may hope to meet him. They found him in some part of the temple, where the doctors of the law kept their schools; he was sitting there, hearkening to their instructions, proposing questions, and answering inquiries, with such wisdom, that those who heard were delighted with him. Young persons should seek the knowledge of Divine truth, attend the ministry of the gospel, and ask such questions of their elders and teachers as may tend to increase their knowledge. Those who seek Christ in sorrow, shall find him with the greater joy. Know ye not that I ought to be in my Father's house; at my Father's work; I must be about my Father's business. Herein is an example; for it becomes the children of God, in conformity to Christ, to attend their heavenly Father's business, and make all other concerns give way to it. Though he was the Son of God, yet he was subject to his earthly parents; how then will the foolish and weak sons of men answer it, who are disobedient to their parents? However we may neglect men's sayings, because they are obscure, yet we must not think so of God's sayings. That which at first is dark, may afterwards become plain and easy. The greatest and wisest, those most eminent, may learn of this admirable and Divine Child, that it is the truest greatness of soul to know our own place and office; to deny ourselves amusements and pleasures not consistent with our state and calling.

John the Baptist's ministry (verses 1–14)

The purpose of John's ministry was to turn people away from their sins and toward the Savior.

He did not preach loyalty to a sect or party, but a profession of repentance.

Baptism with water was the outward sign.

John taught that repentance was necessary for the forgiveness of sins. Washing with water represented the inward cleansing and renewal of heart that accompanies or results from genuine repentance, as well as a public profession of it.

John fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah 40:3.

Preparing the way for the gospel in someone's heart means bringing down proud thoughts, submitting them to Christ and removing what obstructs the coming of his grace.

John gave warnings and practical instructions.

Fallen humanity has become a brood of vipers, corrupt and hostile even toward one another.

The only escape from coming judgment is repentance, shown by a changed way of life.

Neither religious profession nor membership in the visible people of God is of any value without holiness of heart and conduct.

Such privilege only makes judgment more serious if we do not produce fruit worthy of repentance.

John addressed different kinds of people according to their circumstances and occupations.

Anyone claiming repentance must show it through a reformed life appropriate to their responsibilities.

The gospel calls us to mercy rather than empty sacrifice, doing every possible good and treating everyone justly.

The same principle that makes a person refuse dishonest gain also leads that person to restore what was gained by wrongdoing.

John gave soldiers particular instructions suited to the temptations of their work.

His answers both explained immediate duties and tested the sincerity of those asking.

No one can genuinely receive salvation through Christ without repentance, and the marks of that repentance can be seen in such actions.

The joy of Jesus and his disciples (verses 17–24)

Every victory over Satan comes through power received from Jesus.

He must receive all the praise.

Beware of spiritual pride, which has destroyed many.

Jesus rejoiced in the prospect of many people being saved.

The Gospel particularly records this moment of joy.

There were relatively few such moments for him, because he was a Man of Sorrows.

Yet in the hour he learned of the disciples' success and saw Satan's power being defeated, he rejoiced.

God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble.

The more simply we depend upon the Son of God for teaching, help and blessing, the more we will know both Father and Son.

We will enjoy the sight of our Savior's glory and the hearing of his words and become more useful in advancing his cause.

Jesus tells the parable of the good Samaritan (verses 25–37)

We must never speak carelessly about eternal life and the way to receive it.

Such careless speech dishonors God.

No one can love God and neighbor with pure spiritual love without God's converting grace.

The proud human heart resists this truth.

Jesus described a Jewish traveler robbed, wounded and left nearly dead.

He was neglected by people who should have been his friends.

He received help instead from a Samaritan, someone belonging to a nation Jews deeply despised.

How sorrowful to see selfishness in people of every social rank!

How many excuses do we make to avoid trouble or expense in helping someone else?

The genuine Christian has the law of love written on the heart.

The Spirit of Christ lives within, renewing Christ's image in the soul.

This parable explains loving our neighbors as ourselves without regard to nation, faction or other divisions.

It also illustrates the kindness of God our Savior toward sinful and miserable people.

We resemble the wounded traveler.

Satan, our enemy, has robbed and harmed us through sin.

The blessed Jesus looked on us with compassion.

He loved us and gave his life for us while we were his enemies and rebels.

Having shown us mercy, he commands us to go and do likewise.

Each of us, according to our opportunities and abilities, must help people who are in distress and need.

Jesus visits Martha and Mary (verses 38–42)

A good sermon is not made worse simply because it is preached in a private home.

Visits among friends should be arranged so they contribute to the good of people's souls.

To sit at Jesus' feet means readiness to receive his word and submit to its direction.

Martha was preparing food and hospitality for Jesus and those with him.

Her care expressed genuine respect for her Lord and proper concern for her household.

Yet her conduct also deserved correction.

She wanted much serving: plenty of food, variety and careful attention to every detail.

Earthly responsibilities become a trap when they keep us from serving God or receiving spiritual good.

Even when hosting fellow believers, we can waste needless time and money on elaborate arrangements.

Martha was wrong on this occasion, but she remained a genuine believer.

Henry does not claim that her ordinary life neglected the one essential thing.

God's favor is necessary for happiness; Christ's salvation is necessary for safety.

When these are our first concerns, we can attend to other matters properly.

Mary chose the good portion by submitting herself to Christ's instruction.

The things of this world will eventually be taken from us, or we will be taken from them.

But nothing can separate us from Christ's love and the share we possess in it.

Neither human beings nor demons can take it away; God and Christ will not take it away.

Let us therefore give the one essential thing our deepest attention.

Verses 17-24
All our victories over Satan, are obtained by power derived from Jesus Christ, and he must have all the praise. But let us beware of spiritual pride, which has been the destruction of many. Our Lord rejoiced at the prospect of the salvation of many souls. It was fit that particular notice should be taken of that hour of joy; there were few such, for He was a man of sorrows: in that hour in which he saw Satan fall, and heard of the good success of his ministers, in that hour he rejoiced. He has ever resisted the proud, and given grace to the humble. The more simply dependent we are on the teaching, help, and blessing of the Son of God, the more we shall know both of the Father and of the Son; the more blessed we shall be in seeing the glory, and hearing the words of the Divine Saviour; and the more useful we shall be made in promoting his cause.
[Luke.10.25-Luke.10.37]
Verses 25-37
If we speak of eternal life, and the way to it, in a careless manner, we take the name of God in vain. No one will ever love God and his neighbour with any measure of pure, spiritual love, who is not made a partaker of converting grace. But the proud heart of man strives hard against these convictions. Christ gave an instance of a poor Jew in distress, relieved by a good Samaritan. This poor man fell among thieves, who left him about to die of his wounds. He was slighted by those who should have been his friends, and was cared for by a stranger, a Samaritan, of the nation which the Jews most despised and detested, and would have no dealings with. It is lamentable to observe how selfishness governs all ranks; how many excuses men will make to avoid trouble or expense in relieving others. But the true Christian has the law of love written in his heart. The Spirit of Christ dwells in him; Christ's image is renewed in his soul. The parable is a beautiful explanation of the law of loving our neighbour as ourselves, without regard to nation, party, or any other distinction. It also sets forth the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward sinful, miserable men. We were like this poor, distressed traveller. Satan, our enemy, has robbed us, and wounded us: such is the mischief sin has done us. The blessed Jesus had compassion on us. The believer considers that Jesus loved him, and gave his life for him, when an enemy and a rebel; and having shown him mercy, he bids him go and do likewise. It is the duty of us all , in our places, and according to our ability, to succour, help, and relieve all that are in distress and necessity.
[Luke.10.38-Luke.10.42]
Verses 38-42
A good sermon is not the worse for being preached in a house; and the visits of our friends should be so managed, as to make them turn to the good of their souls. Sitting at Christ's feet, signifies readiness to receive his word, and submission to the guidance of it. Martha was providing for the entertainment of Christ, and those that came with him. Here were respect to our Lord Jesus and right care of her household affairs. But there was something to be blamed. She was for much serving; plenty, variety, and exactness. Worldly business is a snare to us, when it hinders us from serving God, and getting good to our souls. What needless time is wasted, and expense often laid out, even in entertaining professors of the gospel! Though Martha was on this occasion faulty, yet she was a true believer, and in her general conduct did not neglect the one thing needful. The favour of God is needful to our happiness; the salvation of Christ is needful to our safety. Where this is attended to, all other things will be rightly pursued. Christ declared, Mary hath chosen the good part. For one thing is needful, this one thing that she has done, to give up herself to the guidance of Christ. The things of this life will be taken away from us, at the furthest, when we shall be taken away from them; but nothing shall separate from the love of Christ, and a part in that love. Men and devils cannot take it away from us, and God and Christ will not. Let us mind the one thing needful more diligently.
